scenario: AITA for not wanting to be friends with my group anymore? | So I just finished my freshman year in college, and I found myself a pretty good friend group. I’ve always been really shy so the fact that I‘m part of a group means a lot to me. However, I’m the only one (in a group of 8) that is not in our school’s Honors College. Many people, including them, have assured me that this doesn’t mean they’re smarter than me or harder working than me, and I’ve accepted that. However, Honors College people all have some required courses to take that are just for them, so they all have classes together without me. And sometimes when we hang out, everyone talks about their classes and I feel completely left out. In addition, I found out that next year, they’re all living in the Honors College dorm building together. I can’t live there since I’m not in Honors College and I already feel left out enough. Now that they’ll all live together, it’s even more likely they’ll end up hanging out without me just because they’re all living together and just happen to run into each other and how can I blame them for that?? I have tried to talk to a couple of them about it and one in particular said that I have no right to make them feel bad for being happy that they can live together but I feel like if they had an ounce of empathy, they’d realize that 7 people of an 8 person group living together is rather unfair. I don’t want to have to start over and find new friends but I also feel like I deserve friends who will try to include me. AITA?

The friends have required courses that the individual isn't taking, so when they hang out, the friends talk about their classes, and the person feels left out. That makes sense because when people have shared experiences, they tend to bond over them, and being excluded from that conversation can feel isolating. Next, the friends are all moving into the Honors College dorm building together. The individual can't live there because they're not in the Honors College. This is a big deal because living together makes it easier for the friends to hang out more frequently. The person is worried that this will lead to them being excluded even more because the friends will naturally run into each other more often. They tried talking to a couple of friends about it, and one of them said they shouldn't feel bad for being happy about living together. The person feels that their friends lack empathy because 7 out of 8 people living together seems unfair. Now, considering whether the person is AITA. Let's think about the dynamics here. The person is feeling excluded because their friends are in a situation that allows them to spend more time together. They tried to express their feelings, but one friend responded by saying they shouldn't feel bad. That could come off as dismissive, but maybe the friend was trying to say that they're happy about their own situation and not trying to hurt the person. On the other hand, the person is feeling that their friends aren't making an effort to include them, especially since they're all moving together. It's a tough spot because the friends might not realize how much their living situation affects the person. They might think that the person is okay with it since they've been assured before, but the person's feelings are valid because the situation has changed. Is the person being unreasonable? They don't want to start over and find new friends, which is understandable. They value their current group and don't want to lose them. At the same time, they feel they deserve friends who make an effort to include them. That seems reasonable. The person is feeling left out both academically and socially. It's natural to feel that way when a significant change like moving happens. They're not asking their friends to give up their opportunities, just to be considerate of their feelings. So, in terms of AITA, I don't think the person is the asshole here. They're expressing valid concerns about feeling excluded, and they've tried to communicate their feelings. The friends might need to be more empathetic and make an effort to include the person, even if it's a bit inconvenient for them. It's a tough situation, but the person's feelings are justified.
